title: “YOUR POSTS ARE TOO LONG!” — BUT WHEN DID WE BECOME TOO BUSY TO READ ABOUT THE GOD WHO GAVE HIS LIFE FOR US?
paragraphs: “YOUR POSTS ARE TOO LONG!” — BUT WHEN DID WE BECOME TOO BUSY TO READ ABOUT THE GOD WHO GAVE HIS LIFE FOR US?

Others judge before reaching the final paragraph. But somewhere, someone is reading every word because they are desperate for the biblical truth, hope, and understanding that might help them take one more step toward Jesus.
I have heard the complaints.
“Your posts are too long.”
“Can you make them shorter?”
“People don't have time to read all that.”
And sometimes, before someone has even finished reading the article, they have already formed an opinion about what I supposedly meant.
They see a sentence. They react to it. They assume they understand the entire message.
Then they argue against a conclusion I never actually made.
I won't pretend that never gets discouraging.

Because behind some of these long articles are hours of studying, examining Scripture, checking context, questioning my own assumptions, praying for wisdom, and trying to explain something that cannot always be faithfully communicated in three sentences.
But I want to say something, not out of anger, not out of pride, and certainly not because I believe everyone owes me their attention.
I want to say it because I believe we are slowly losing something precious.
The willingness to slow down long enough to understand.
And perhaps the saddest part is that this problem doesn't stop with social media.
Sometimes, we bring the same impatience into our relationship with God.
We want a quick promise without understanding the covenant.
We want encouragement without correction.
We want the comfort of grace without examining why we desperately need it.
We want the resurrection without spending time at the cross.
We want a verse that makes us feel better, but we struggle to sit with a passage that challenges the way we live.
And somewhere along the way, we begin confusing a message that is easy to consume with a message that is spiritually nourishing.
Please understand me.
A short message is not automatically shallow, and a long message is not automatically deep.
Jesus Himself spoke words of extraordinary power in remarkably few sentences.
The thief on the cross did not need a lengthy theological lecture to hear the Savior's promise of paradise (Luke 23:42–43).
The tax collector in Jesus' parable cried, “God be merciful to me a sinner” (Luke 18:13, KJV), and Jesus said he went home justified.
The Gospel can be proclaimed simply and faithfully.
But Scripture also contains long sermons, extended arguments, detailed histories, poetry, prophecy, difficult teachings, and letters that require careful attention.
Paul did not always explain profound truths in catchy little slogans.
The author of Hebrews did not reduce the priesthood of Christ to a motivational caption.
And when Jesus walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, He did not merely give them a comforting phrase and send them on their way.
Luke 24:27 says:
“And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.” (KJV)
Imagine that journey.
Two discouraged disciples.
Their hopes apparently buried with Jesus.
Their understanding shattered by the crucifixion.
And the risen Christ walking beside them, patiently opening the Scriptures and showing them how the story pointed to Him.
He did not merely address their emotions.
He corrected their understanding.
He showed them that the suffering of the Messiah was not the failure of God's plan.
It was central to its fulfillment.
Later, they said:
“Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?” (Luke 24:32, KJV)
Their hearts burned as Christ opened the Scriptures.
Not because the explanation was designed to entertain them.
But because the truth revealed the Savior they had failed to recognize.
And that is what I pray happens when someone reads something I have written.
Not that they become impressed with my vocabulary.
Not that they admire how long I can write.
Not that they agree with everything I say.
But that somewhere in the explanation, they begin to see Jesus more clearly.
That a person struggling with shame discovers the grace of Christ.
That someone who has misunderstood repentance begins to understand why turning from sin is not the enemy of grace but a proper response to it.
That a wounded believer discovers that forgiveness is possible.
That someone who has spent years hearing Bible verses without understanding their context finally begins to see how they fit into the larger story of redemption.
And that someone who has almost abandoned the faith finds a reason to open the Bible again.
That is worth more to me than producing something people can finish in ten seconds.
There is a Greek word in 2 Timothy 2:15 that I want you to notice.
ὀρθοτομοῦντα — orthotomounta.
It comes from the verb orthotomeō, literally carrying the idea of cutting straight, and in this passage referring to handling or teaching the word of truth correctly.
Paul writes:
The Greek phrase is:
ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας
Orthotomounta ton logon tēs alētheias.
Correctly handling the word of truth.
Notice something important.
The central concern is not how quickly someone can finish reading.
It is whether the truth is being handled faithfully.
And in the original context, Paul is instructing Timothy as a worker and teacher of God's Word, warning against empty and destructive disputes.
This is not a command requiring every Christian to read long Facebook articles.
But it establishes a principle that should matter to anyone teaching Scripture.
Accuracy matters. Context matters. Truth matters.
And sometimes, explaining a biblical truth responsibly requires more than a catchy sentence.
Sometimes you need to explain who was speaking.
Who was listening.
What happened before the verse.
What happened after it.
What a word meant in its original context.
How a passage relates to the rest of Scripture.
And most importantly, how we should understand and respond to it in light of Jesus Christ.
Because one of the most dangerous things we can do with the Bible is take a sentence God gave within a larger revelation and force it to say whatever we already wanted to believe.
A verse taken out of context can sound powerful while communicating something the biblical author never intended.
And I would rather take the time to explain a passage carefully than offer a convenient interpretation that misleads someone's soul.
That doesn't mean my explanations are beyond correction.
Far from it.
I am a fellow student of Scripture, dependent on God's mercy, and I must remain willing to be corrected by the Word I seek to teach.
If I misunderstand a passage, show me from Scripture.
If I overlook context, help me examine it.
If I make an unsupported claim, challenge it respectfully.
I welcome thoughtful biblical discussion.
But please, read what I actually wrote before deciding what I believe.
Because there is a difference between correcting an error and reacting to an assumption.
Proverbs 18:13 says:
“He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.” (KJV)
That verse is not specifically about social media.
It is about the foolishness of answering before hearing.
But its wisdom certainly reaches into the way we communicate today.
How many disagreements could be avoided if we listened before responding?
How many believers have been misunderstood because someone reacted to a single sentence while ignoring the explanation surrounding it?
How many arguments are not really disagreements about truth at all, but disagreements with something the other person never said?
And how many times have we ourselves done exactly that?
I have to ask myself that question too.
Because it is easy to demand patience from other people while failing to practice it ourselves.
Now, let me address something else.
If you prefer short posts, that is perfectly fine.
There are many Christian pages, teachers, pastors, and creators sharing brief devotionals, concise biblical reflections, and encouraging reminders.
Some of them do an excellent job.
Follow them.
Read them.
Be encouraged by them.
There is room in the body of Christ for different teaching styles and different ways of communicating biblical truth.
A person who has five minutes between responsibilities may benefit greatly from a short devotional.
A tired parent may only have enough attention for a few verses before going to sleep.
A worker coming home after a long shift may genuinely struggle to concentrate.
A person with reading difficulties may need a different format.
I understand that.
I do not believe someone is less spiritual because they cannot finish one of my articles.
Your ability to read a long post is not a measurement of how much you love Jesus.
And I would never want my writing to become another burden placed on people whom Christ calls to Himself.
But I also want to be clear about something.
I am not trying to make every article fit the attention span of someone who never intended to read it.
My focus is different.
I want to provide deeper explanations for people who are hungry for them.
People who have questions that cannot be answered responsibly in a single paragraph.
People who want to understand difficult passages.
People who are tired of hearing verses quoted without context.
People who are preparing Bible studies, sermons, devotionals, and discipleship lessons.
People who want more than an emotional moment.
They want understanding that can shape their lives.
And I have heard from readers who use these articles as study aids, sermon preparation references, and resources for discipleship.
That humbles me.
Because it also reminds me of the responsibility involved.
If someone is going to use an article in teaching others, the article must be examined carefully against Scripture.
No Gospel Warrior article should replace personal Bible study, responsible interpretation, or the faithful teaching and accountability of a local church.
But if something I write can help a believer ask better questions, understand a passage more accurately, or point someone toward Christ, then I am grateful.
And if one person reads a long article and comes away understanding the Gospel more clearly, the effort was worthwhile.
Now, here is something I sometimes say with a little smile.
My posts are still shorter than the Bible.
Yes, I know.
Someone reading this might already be thinking, “Here he goes again.”
But hear the heart behind that statement.
I am not saying my articles carry the authority of Scripture.
They do not.
The Bible is God's inspired Word. My articles are human explanations that must be tested by it.
And I am certainly not saying that finishing my posts is equivalent to reading Scripture.
It isn't.
What I am saying is that perhaps we can begin practicing a little more patience with longer, thoughtful reading.
Not because length itself makes us holy.
But because sustained attention can help us engage more carefully with complicated ideas.
If we struggle to concentrate, we can grow.
We can read a little today.
Return tomorrow.
Pause and think.
Open the verses being discussed.
Check the context.
Ask questions.
And slowly rebuild the habit of engaging deeply instead of constantly moving on to the next thing.
Spiritual maturity does not come from reading more words on a screen.
It comes through God's grace as His Spirit works in us through His Word, prayer, obedience, fellowship, and the other means by which He nurtures His people.
But learning to give careful attention to Scripture is part of that growth.
Consider what happened in Nehemiah 8.
The people gathered to hear the Law of God.
Ezra read from the book.
And Nehemiah 8:8 says:
“So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” (KJV)
They did not merely hear words.
They were helped to understand their meaning.
In the Hebrew text, the word מְפֹרָשׁ — meforash is associated with making the reading clear or distinct, while the wider verse emphasizes giving the sense so that the people understood.
There are interpretive discussions about precisely how that clarity was provided, including whether translation or explanation was involved.
But the central picture is unmistakable.
God's Word was read, and the people were helped to understand it.
That matters.
Because hearing a verse and understanding a verse are not always the same thing.
And sometimes the difference between confusion and clarity is someone taking the time to explain.
I think about the Ethiopian official in Acts 8.
He was reading the prophet Isaiah.
Philip approached him and asked:
“Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Acts 8:30, KJV)
The man answered:
“How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Acts 8:31, KJV)
And Philip began with that Scripture and preached Jesus to him.
What a beautiful moment.
A man was reading the Bible but needed help understanding whom the passage was describing.
Philip did not mock him for asking questions.
He did not shame him for needing an explanation.
He met him where he was and pointed him to Christ.
That is the kind of teaching I want to pursue.
Not teaching that makes people dependent on my page.
Teaching that helps them become more rooted in Scripture and more devoted to Jesus.
Not explanations that make people say, “I could never understand the Bible without this writer.”
But explanations that encourage them to open the Bible themselves.
To study.
To pray.
To ask.
To grow.
And eventually, perhaps, to help someone else understand.
Because discipleship is not supposed to end with consuming content.
It is supposed to shape the way we follow Christ.
And there is something else I want to say to the person who is still reading.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be misunderstood.
You tried to explain your heart, but someone only heard the part that offended them.
You wrote a message trying to make peace, but the other person focused on one sentence.
You shared your testimony, but someone reduced your entire life to your worst mistake.
You tried to tell people what God was doing in you, but they could only remember who you used to be.
And now you hesitate to speak.
Because you are tired of being judged by people who never stayed long enough to understand your story.
If that is you, I want to point you to Someone who knows what it means to be falsely accused and misunderstood.
Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God was rejected, mocked, falsely accused, and condemned.
But there is an important difference between His suffering and ours.
We are imperfect people who sometimes contribute to our own misunderstandings.
Jesus was without sin.
He did not suffer because He needed to repent.
He suffered as the righteous Savior who came to redeem sinners.
And at the cross, something happened far greater than the correction of a misunderstanding.
The Son of God gave His life for our sins.
He bore the judgment our rebellion deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that God finally understood our side of the story.
He already knows us completely.
The miracle is that the holy God who knows the full truth about our sin has made forgiveness and reconciliation possible through Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we fixed our reputations.
Not after we learned to explain ourselves perfectly.
Not after we convinced everyone that we were worth loving.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And that brings me back to the reason this ministry carries the words:
Those words are not a claim that the past never happened.
They are not permission to hide wrongdoing.
They do not mean repentance is unnecessary or that the consequences of sin always disappear.
They mean that through Jesus Christ, sin and shame do not have to be the final chapter.
The person who repents and trusts in Christ receives forgiveness.
The guilty can be justified.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The broken can be restored.
The sinner can become a new creation.
As 2 Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
That is why I write.
Not merely to defend long articles.
Not to win arguments with people who prefer shorter posts.
Not to prove that my style is better than someone else's.
I write because the Gospel is too precious to treat carelessly.
And because somewhere beyond the complaints, there are people who need patient, Scripture-centered teaching.
A young believer trying to understand grace.
A father preparing to lead his family in Bible study.
A mother praying for a child who has wandered from God.
A preacher preparing a message and looking for a clearer understanding of a passage.
A new Christian trying to distinguish biblical truth from popular religious sayings.
A struggling believer who has read the same verse for years but never understood its context.
A person silently battling guilt who needs to hear that forgiveness is found in Christ.
And maybe someone who has never truly understood why Jesus had to die.
If a longer explanation helps one of those people, then I do not consider those words wasted.
But I also need to remember something.
Even the most carefully written article cannot save a soul.
Jesus saves.
A powerful sentence cannot regenerate a heart.
The Holy Spirit gives life.
An emotional story cannot replace repentance and faith.
Only Christ can reconcile us to God.
So if you ever finish one of my articles remembering my writing more than you remember the Savior, then I have not accomplished what I most deeply wanted to accomplish.
The purpose is not to make Gospel Warrior famous. The purpose is to make Jesus Christ known.
Some people assume that because a ministry shares Christian teaching online, there should never be any financial support involved.
Others have seen so much manipulation and misuse of money in religious spaces that they have become understandably cautious.
I understand those concerns.
Christian ministry should never exploit fear, guilt, or people's desire to please God.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
And no one should ever be made to feel that paying a ministry is a condition of faithful discipleship.
But Scripture does teach that those who benefit from spiritual instruction may freely and generously support those who labor in teaching.
Galatians 6:6 says:
“Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.” (KJV)
In this context, communicate refers to sharing or participating in material support.
Paul also writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
Notice the balance.
Supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful act of generosity and service to God.
But biblical giving is not supposed to be extracted through pressure.
That is why I want to invite you, not manipulate you.
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and wise stewardship still matter.
And you do not need to be wealthy to make a difference.
Consistent support from people who believe in the mission can help a ministry continue serving.
Those products are not the Gospel.
God's Word is not reserved for paying members.
I want people to know about that library because I do not want anyone to assume that growing in biblical understanding must depend on having money.
If you are serious about going deeper in your walk with Christ, make use of the free resources.
Study carefully.
Compare teachings with Scripture.
Share what is helpful.
And keep growing.
But perhaps one friend will read it.
Perhaps someone in your family has been quietly asking questions about God.
Perhaps a struggling believer will encounter a passage that encourages them to return to Scripture.
Perhaps someone will recognize a misunderstanding they have carried for years.
Perhaps a person who has been avoiding church will begin reconsidering the claims of Jesus Christ.
We cannot control what God will do through something we share.
But we can faithfully offer what we have.
Not because you owe me publicity.
But because someone in your circle might benefit from the biblical conversation.
Invite them to examine the Scriptures with us.
If you know someone who usually prefers short devotionals but has been wanting to grow in deeper Bible study, invite them too, without pressuring them.
They do not have to agree with everything before they begin reading.
Honest questions are welcome.
Not just a quick reaction.
I want to know something meaningful.
Have you ever been misunderstood because someone judged your words before hearing your full explanation?
Or have you ever discovered that a Bible passage meant something deeper, richer, or different from what you originally assumed after studying its context?
Tell me about it.
If you use these longer Gospel Warrior articles in sermons, personal study, small groups, or discipleship, I would love to hear how they have helped you—and what could be improved.
And if you have struggled to remain patient with longer biblical teaching, you can be honest about that too.
There is no shame in admitting that you are still learning.
You can simply comment, “Lord, teach me to love Your Word.”
Not as a performance for other people.
As a sincere prayer.
Because the goal is not to become someone who can boast about reading long posts.
The goal is to become someone who knows Christ more deeply and handles His Word more faithfully.
And to those who have stayed with me through these long articles, I want to say thank you.
Thank you for reading beyond the first paragraph.
Thank you for checking the passages.
Thank you for asking thoughtful questions.
Thank you for encouraging me when the work feels exhausting.
Thank you for correcting me when correction is needed.
Thank you for using these writings as a doorway into Scripture rather than a replacement for it.
Your messages and testimonies remind me that meaningful ministry cannot always be measured by likes, shares, or the number of people who reach the end of a post.
Sometimes the most meaningful fruit is something no algorithm can measure.
A believer returning to prayer.
A family opening the Bible together.
A sinner recognizing the need to repent.
A wounded person learning to trust Christ again.
A disciple growing in understanding.
And someone finally realizing that Christianity is not merely a collection of inspirational sayings.
It is the announcement of what God has accomplished through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
So yes, I will continue working on making my writing clearer.
I will keep learning how to remove unnecessary words.
I will try to avoid repetition that does not help the message.
I will work to make difficult ideas easier to understand.
Because good teaching should respect the reader's time.
But I will not deliberately remove essential context merely to make every article fit into a few seconds of scrolling.
Some truths can be explained briefly.
Others deserve a longer conversation.
And I believe there is room for both.
If you prefer shorter posts, I respect that.
If you love deeper articles, you are welcome here.
If you disagree, let us examine the Scriptures together.
If you are struggling, you do not have to pretend.
If you have wandered from God, the call of the Gospel is still to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
And if you have been wounded by the judgment of others, remember that your deepest hope is not found in getting everyone to understand your story.
Your hope is found in the Savior who knows the whole truth about you and is mighty to save.
Because ultimately, this conversation is not about the length of my Facebook posts.
It is about what we are willing to give our attention to.
We live in a world full of noise.
Endless opinions.
Endless arguments.
Endless distractions.
And a thousand things competing for the few quiet moments we have.
But Jesus Christ remains worthy of our attention.
His Word remains worthy of careful study.
His cross remains worthy of proclamation.
His resurrection remains the foundation of Christian hope.
And His grace remains sufficient for sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
So the next time you see one of my long articles, you do not have to read it immediately.
You can save it.
Come back when you have time.
Open your Bible beside it.
Read it in portions.
Question what I have written.
Test it against Scripture.
And if you discover that I have explained something incorrectly, let us seek the truth together.
Because I would rather be corrected by Scripture than applauded for an error.
And I would rather help one person understand Jesus faithfully than gain a thousand reactions from a message that distorts His Word.
I am not asking you to worship long articles.
I am asking you not to confuse brevity with truth or length with uselessness.
And above all, I am inviting you to know the One whom all faithful Christian teaching should proclaim.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who entered our broken world.
The Lamb of God who takes away sin.
The risen Lord who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His finished work.
The Redeemer who transforms lives by grace.
The One who can take a story marked by shame and write a new chapter of redemption.
If this ministry helps you see Him more clearly, then every hour of careful study, every revision, and every thoughtfully written paragraph has a purpose.
But whatever you decide about my writing, do not miss the greater invitation.
Open the Scriptures.
Seek the Lord.
Turn from sin.
Trust in Jesus Christ.
And keep following Him.
